newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures settled little changed after calm session with traders and analysts waiting for some more solid signals from the United States to shake the market out of its current range.

Traders said the December contract had solid support around 127.34/36 but would be unlikely to break above resistance at 127.48/52 without external help, partly because the recent flow of demand for bonds from domestic investors had slowed.
They said investors remained reluctant to buy with the long-bond yields hovering at their lowest levels since February 1994, finding 10-year yields below six percent hard to stomach.
The mixed signals from the U.S. October producer price index left bond prices little changed and there was little reaction to the weak Atlanta Fed business activity index.

Although the headline PPI rise of 0.4 percent was stronger than expected the fact temporary oil price rises fueled much of the increase left traders neutral, waiting for the U.S. consumer price index on Thursday.
"The was a little disappointment there wasn't a better figure to push the market up," a trader at a French brokerage said. "Now we wait for the CPI and retail sales but it's very, very quiet."
Few expected a shock rate rise from the U.S. Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee meeting on Wednesday although some said there was a prospect of a rise by the end of the year.
"Most people don't believe in a move at all," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro in Paris. "But the risk is not zero."
French welfare debt repayment fund CADES had no trouble selling 9.97 billion francs of its 2002, 2005 and 2007 bonds at auction on Wednesday.
However traders and analysts cautioned against reading too much into the relatively high bid-to-cover ratio.
A bond trader at a French bank said bidding for the quasi-government CADES bonds was almost a political issue for primary dealers, as at regular government auctions.
An added incentive to bid was the fact CADES would almost certainly be awarding more mandates to primary dealers for syndicated issues in the future, he said.
The high 5.1 bid-to-cover ratio for the 2005 bond was boosted by bids as high as 101.72, a long way above the lowest accepted price of 101.54.
"I think the demand was mostly professional with very little final demand," a trader at a U.S. bank in Paris said.
However, he said there had been relatively good demand, especially for the 2002 bond, from investors in the run up to the auction.

The 10-year spread between French and German government bond yields ended unchanged at parity although French bonds had lagged Bunds for most of the day. The two-, five- and 30-year spreads also ended unchanged from Tuesday.
Brossard at ABN Amro said the French government's release of its revised 1996 budget, reaffirming the central government budget deficit forecast at 288 billion francs, was mildly favourable news.
"There is a serious question mark over how they will make their savings" to offset extra spending, "but one imagines it's possible to do so," Brossard said.

He said the fact the government still expected to be on target is "rather good news at this stage of the year and encouraging for 1997," especially as the original budget was based on over optimistic growth forecasts.
The franc was little changed against the mark at 3.3798 and December PIBOR remained penned into a tight two-basis point range all day.
-- David Clarke, Paris Newsroom +331 4221 5542
